have been carted away to work in the mines in Europe, and that is the truth. We would have had the horror of war on our own soil.
I am very much surprised at what the government has done for the people of this country in these Geneva pacts, and that we should have this discussion in the house. I am speaking for myself alone and not for any others. I am opposed to any action that affects adversely the mother country, such as the removal of preferences.
In conclusion, I wish to say that these Geneva pacts were founded on the Bretton Woods agreement and the United States loan, which I apposed here. They met at Geneva for six months. All we heard about it was the announcement over the radio on November 17. I for one do not intend to see the economy of this country so changed that the trade with the best customer we ever had, Britain, will be lost. The mother country has been our best customer for grain, bacon, eggs and other products. I am not going to see it thrown away to the four winds of heaven for any Geneva pact, because we have had hundreds of these. The gentlemen are now meeting down in Havana. In his own name Mr. Wilgress made an announcement over the head of the government, saying what the government was going to do. It is time for us to recover our responsibility as private members. If we do not resume our responsibilities the day of parliamentary government will be gone.
M*. J. H. FERGUSON (Simcoe North): Mr. Speaker, I cannot see my way clear to vote for this bill; first, because I do not believe that the present government is capable of entering into international negotiations based on such a bill which will produce anything but terrible chaos. The example set by this government in Canada is comparatively poor, and the effects comparatively small, compared with what might result from the signing of the Geneva convention. This country is in the mess in which it finds itself because the present cabinet were imbued with the idea around election time that, if elected, and appointed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), their duties were to sit in certain offices and do their job as they saw fit. These men were elected and appointed, and they sat in offices. From the conditions we find in Canada today in practically every walk of life it is obvious that they have not handled their positions and their offices with any semblance of business practice or intelligence.
Probably two months ago while attending a protest meeting of a thousand hog raisers in Ontario I listened to apparently a champion and great supporter of the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Abbott). He tried to take the rightful blame from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). He tried to show the audience that the Minister of Agriculture was not to blame for the non-notification that the price of hog feed might go up. He tried to show that the Minister of Finance was entirely to blame. I might say I followed the speaker and emphasized1 the fact that they could not place this muddle on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance; that the blame should go where it should1 be properly placed, namely, on the shoulders of the Minister of Agriculture.
It now appears that all ministers of the crown are attempting to bring in the old saying, "Let George do it." The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is the greatest "George" I have ever seen or have ever known. He is now being the "George" for the Department of Finance. He is the one man that the Minister of Finance prays and hopes cam help him out of the muddle in which he and his department, through his efforts, have placed Canada, for the first time in its history, namely, borrowing money from a foreign government. The people of Canada must love the position in which they find themselves. No longer are our securities being sought by private investors.
I hold in my hand a label from a lowly can of pork and beans. Beans are grown abundantly in Canada, and our hogs are second to none. Yet the purchasing public of Canada must buy on the grocery shelves pork and beans which are grown and canned in the state of New York in the United States. Here is another label of a can of corn. The corn was grown in the state of Maryland. Here is another label from a humble bottle of catsup grown and canned in New Jersey. I say that this is all brought about by the fact that during the war Canadians were made leaners to some extent by having to rely on the guidance and control of the present government, instead of this government aiding the manufacturers, the farmers and the labour people to get back on their own feet, work and get themselves out of their difficulty. The government have made no effort to do that. They have kept them in the dark. They have gathered statistics covering every phase of Canadian life by the bureau of statistics in Ottawa, and they have imparted none of the findings of these research men.
Recently a friend of mine made a small addition to his home. I will show the house how far these statistics go. I hold in my hand a sheaf of literature in which they asked the gentleman in question fifty or sixty questions why he built his house; how much it cost

him; whether he intended to build any more; and who supplied the materials. He was told that if he did1 not answer these questions he was liable to a penalty of S100 or three months in jail. I feel quite confident that the same kind of questionnaire goes to every supposedly free Canadian, and when this literature is compiled' by these experts, it is kept in the archives in Ottawa. I am sure it never brings any benefits to the people of Canada, whom this government is supposed to represent. No one who during the war was desirous of producing for the benefit of Canada, the empire and the world at large ever received the vaguest information, as to what he should produce to the maximum, or in what commodity there would likely be over-production and on which he should go easy. The same tendency has been evident in Canada since the war. The farmer has never been warned by the statistical branch through the ministers of the crown, that he might be over-producing in wheat or some other commodity in the light of any facts which the government might see fit to put before him. The farmers have been ignored by the government. They have never had the slightest intimation that hog feed was becoming scarce, either in consequence of a drought or owdng to other conditions in the western provinces or throughout the world. They have never had the slightest intimation that higher prices would be asked for so far as farmers products are concerned. The farmer did not know what to do with his brood sows, and the net result will be that the government will be on its knees crying for bacon for the Canadian people, to say nothing of the export trade.
Let us hope that this is not the last straw that will break the camel's back, which straw the cabinet ministers are now putting on the shoulders of "George" Howe-

There is no satisfaction in saying "I told you so", when a calamity has happened, and it is only worthwhile to go over past history in the hope that the trend may be altered and the greater calamity which faces us may be prevented. I am, therefore, going to retrace briefly the history of what has taken place with regard to our exchange position, dating from the very great mistake of putting the Canadian dollar at par on July S, 194&. At that time the situation was that we .were completely out of debt, or at least our federal government was completely out of external debt. It was out of foreign debt, and we had a surplus of gold and hard currency amounting to about one billion and two-thirds; I believe the amount was approximately SI,600,000,000.
Since then, as is known, we have incurred, for the first time in our history, I believe, an obligation on the part of the federal government to another government. We have dissipated virtually our entire stock of hard currency and gold, and we are running into the red in our trading position at the rate, before the recent embargoes were put on, of approximately one billion dollars a year. Since this has happened there has been an improvement, but that improvement is not great enough to put our position in balance with regard to our trading position with the United States.
More measures will have to be taken or more debts incurred. There is no other way out of the impasse in which this country finds itself. I have frequently warned the government that it would have to take three steps. Of these they have taken two, and the third

Foreign Exchange Conservation
they will, in my opinion, be forced to take. They have taken the step of imposing tariffs by embargo. They have taken the step of imposing wartime restrictions as to the export of United States or hard currency, and recently they have even tightened up the export of gold bullion in semi-manufactured state. They were forced to take these steps.
The other step which they have not taken and which, in my opinion, they will be forced to take is devaluation. No matter what they may say; no matter what announcements may come from the Department of Finance, devaluation will eventually be forced on the government.
On July 5, 1946, the parity move was made. At that time I suggested that that move was brought about by pressure from the Washington government. This was denied in the house by the then minister of finance. Subsequently to that, a motion was brought forward by this government to bonus the production of gold, which would have had the effect of currency devaluation. The United States government immediately raised the most strenuous objections, so much so that, together with the objection raised by the mining industry, the plan was dropped. We must accept the word of the government that no pressure was brought on them in 1946. But it is extremely strange, Mr. Speaker, that if no pressure had been brought on in 1946, how vehement and how violent was pressure from Washington with regard to a similar measure a few months later.
The next thing that happened was that in July of last year I again warned that this government could not meet its external balance of trade. A great deal of confidence was put on the convertibility of sterling. I warned that the convertibility of sterling was a myth. The chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Dalton, said that sterling would be made convertible and he was sure that it would be made to stick. That, just like our parity action, was purely wishful thinking. Sterling was made convertible, and within a few days the drain on the British economy was so great that sterling had to go back to its inconvertibility. Today we see a similar pressure being built up. The first country to devalue some months ago, while not a member of the international monetary fund, was Italy. Immediately Italy put its currency on a more realistic basis, despite the chaotic condition within that country, prosperity began to return, factories began to work and production began to increase. As I have said, that was despite the chaotic political internal condition in the country.

speechtext:
Then we come to France. On the last day of the short session before Christmas I warned that a wave of devaluation would sweep across the countries of the world and that it might start before we came back to this house. Quite conveniently it started on the day we actually came back. France devalued and put her currency on a realistic basis. I predict that the result will be prosperity, increased production and that we shall begin to see French goods and French textiles becoming a factor again in the world market.
Today England stubbornly refuses to devalue because of a socialist ideology. For the same reason that the ex-chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Dalton, refused to admit the dangers of making sterling convertible into dollars, today Sir Stafford Cripps is saying that the pound will not be devalued. It is just like trying to tell water to run uphill, as to say that the pound will not be devalued. When it will happen, I do not know. But let me say this: today the cost of English goods in this country, aggravated by this measure, is so great that last week in Toronto a textile salesman from one of the largest houses in Great Britain was unable to sell any of his goods because he could not meet the prices at which we were able and willing to buy. That is a sign of what will happen.
I am informed that steam turbines from England are now offered at a price that is as much as thirty to forty per cent higher than the competitive price in the United States. Furthermore, British shipbuilding is now so greatly inflated that it is impossible to buy a ship in England, without government assistance, and charge rates for freight and passengers which would ever make the investment worthwhile; that is, pay the carrying charges. There is, of course, government assistance to replace ships sunk during the war, and for other war damage. But there is a great and intolerable price rise on goods from England.
To say that the pound is worth $4 when it can be bought for $2.25 and $2.40 at most banks in Canada, if they have any, is just one of those terrific fallacies that all money planners fall into. It is unreal and untrue, and is doing the economy of the United Kingdom incalculable harm, having regard to the trading position between us. Had we taken a realistic view in 1946 and set our dollar free instead of tying it to the United States dollar

Foreign Exchange Conservation
we would still be in possession of a great deal of that valuable nest-egg of hard currency and gold which has been dissipated.
Every time an attempt is made to peg a currency above its real worth, drain is inevitable. It happened in England in 1926. When Winston Churchill put the British pound back on the 1914 gold standard, the drain on British gold wits so great that the measure had to be abandoned within a few years, nearly wrecking the economy of the United Kingdom. We are doing virtually the same thing. Had we devalued or left our currency at 90 cents, United States, it is said that our oil and our coal would have cost us more. Since 1946 our oil and our coal have gone up, depending upon the location, as much as fifty per cent. I understand that in some places they have gone up considerably more than that. To say that devaluation of ten per cent would have materially affected the over-all price of coal and oil, even assuming that it would have put it up ten per cent more than it has already gone up, is to lose sight of reality with regard to the actual price people have to pay for those two vital commodities.
I want to say here, Mr. Speaker, that we on this side of the house have for years pleaded with the government to allow oil drilling and exploration as a 100 per cent deduction from taxation to the companies which were prospecting and drilling for oil. Had that been done, every oil well that we could have got into production in Canada would now have been vital not only in the safeguarding of our exchange position but in the production of essential fuel in this serious crisis.
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to prolong the debate at this moment. I merely say that the present situation is dangerous and unreal; that our trading position is still in imbalance. We are still going into the red in our trade with the United States at an alarming rate, despite the improvement in December; and unless the minister uses the third weapon at his command, that of devaluation, in six months or a year more severe, more vicious and more unpleasant restrictions and regulations are in store for the Canadian people.

I think I have been quite patient in awaiting my turn. I wish only to express my opposition to this bill, briefly, opposition based on the attitude of a goodly number of my constituents who have expressed their opinions through labour organizations, farmers' organizations and co-operatives, and

as individuals. While I am not unmindful of the necessity for foreign exchange conservation, I intend to oppose this bill for the following reasons.
The first is the unwillingness of the government to consider the widespread demand for the importation of some fresh fruits and vegetables. On this question I am sure the minister and the government have overlooked the necessity for such fresh fruits and vegetables, particularly on the part of men engaged in heavy industry, in the lumber industry, in mining and the smelting industry.
The second reason is because of the application of the principle of non-discrimination at this time. On this point a great deal was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) with which I agree, but I am not going to repeat what they had to say.
Then I represent a riding in which a large part of the population strongly resents the fact that apparently the policies of this government are being dovetailed with United States opinions and ideas. Many of my people have the opinion, and feel very keenly about it, that our financial, fiscal and trade policies are being patterned more and more to suit the needs and wishes of the United States.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I intend to oppose this bill because of the government's actions in the whole sphere of conservation and regulation and quotas. There is a definite sense of insecurity among producers. The farmers of my district are not able to plan their production because they do not know how long these regulations will remain in effect. Under present conditions, in the next twelve months there will be a greatly stimulated demand for such vegetables as lettuce, celery, cabbage, carrots and so on, but because of their lack of knowledge of what the future may hold, and that sense of insecurity, the farmers do not know what to do in the planting of certain crops.
Again, I wish to express my opposition to this bill because of the failure on the part of the government to reimpose price ceilings on items under quota and to bring into effect some degree of justice as far as purchasing in this country is concerned.
In conclusion, I must make reference to the excise tax, which has had a serious effect on a good many farmers in my district as well as on many people who are building and furnishing homes. I want particularly to emphasize the effect it has had on various co-operative transportation societies in my riding. In the Rossland-Trail section of my riding we have a number of successful transportation societies, one or two having a large

Foreign Exchange Conservation
capitalization and owning fleets of buses and trucks. I know from personal experience that all during the war these organizations co-operated with the government in every way in refraining from purchasing new vehicles, parts, equipment and so on. Now all their equipment is in poor condition and run down because they conformed to the wishes of fhe government and co-operated in every way. Today they wish to buy new equipment, but they are penalized by this twenty-five pet cent excise tax.
For the reasons I have briefl3r stated, Mr. Speaker, based on complaints presented to me by a large number of my constituents, I intend to oppose this bill on second reading.

A good deal of territory has been covered in the course of this debate, and a good many matters other than those that relate to the bill before the house have been discussed. That is perfectly proper because at the outset, before the Christmas recess, I think it was agreed tacitly, at any rate, that on second reading we would discuss all aspects of the government's exchange conservation program. However, in my remarks in closing the debate I propose to restrict myself as far as possible to this bill. In particular I want to emphasize that, as all hon. members know, in this matter we are voting on the principle of Bill No. 3. That principle is very simple; it is the use of import restrictions in order to conserve United States dollars. One may quarrel with a good deal of the detail; one may consider that this or that article should not be prohibited, this or that article should not be placed under quota and this or that article should not be placed under import permit, but the principle of the bill is simply, do we or do we not use the import restriction method of conserving United States dollars. I consider it important that this should be realized, because that is the principle hon. members will be voting for or against.
I do not think I shall attempt to deal with all the matters that have been raised by hon. members in the course of the debate. A number of them can be more appropriately handled when we are in committee. But there are one or two main points with which I wish to deal, taking first the points raised by the official opposition. All their speakers have said they intend to oppose the bill.

Their attitude has been consistent in that regard. They did not indicate on what grounds they opposed the principle, but at least some of them did advocate or suggest an alternative, namely -the devaluation or depreciation of the Canadian dollar. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) suggested a devaluation of ten per cent, and the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) interjected, "More if necessary." I have already dealt with this question of currency depreciation, when I introduced the bill, but I think I had better say a word or two about it again and of necessity, to some extent repeat what I said at that time.
I said then that currency depreciation may be helpful to a country which is in balance of payment difficulties because its costs and prices are too high to enable it to compete effectively in the export market. Unquestionably a number of countries are today in that position, but Canada is not one of them. We are not precluded1 from exporting our goods to any other country because of price. As a matter of fact, we have, kept our costs relatively low, and at current rates of exchange our staple exports can be and are being exported to any market of the world in competition with any other exporter. In my judgment, inability to export is the only real justification for currency depreciation on the part of any country. Otherwise we would be attempting to obtain an unfair advantage in some export market at the expense of somebody else.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have dealt with this question of currency devaluation in broad, general terms. They have been assertive, but none of them has been able to convince me, and I doubt if they have been able to convince the people of Canada, that a ten per cent currency depreciation would accomplish the restriction on the expenditure of United States dollars which is necessary under existing circumstances. There are only two ways to cure our present position. One is to export more to dollar markets and the other is to import less. The bill which we are now considering deals with the restrictive side of the program, the method whereby the government is proposing a restriction of dollar imports. The constructive side of the program has not been touched upon in the course of this debate, and at this hour I am not going to repeat what I have said on other occasions with respect to that aspect of the government's program.
The bill which we are now considering deals solely with the restrictive side of the program, the method whereby we shall restrict our use of United States dollars. The obvious

inference from the devaluation idea is that it would cause people in Canada to spend less for United States imports, in other words, to reduce their purchases. Well, as I have said before, an increase of some forty to forty-five per cent in the cost of United States imports over the last eighteen months has not produced any appreciable reduction in the scale of our imports.

I repeat what I said earlier, that I do not believe a ten per cent devaluation of our dollar would produce any appreciable effect upon our imports from the United States. That is my belief. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been suggesting that it would, but I make the assertion that it would not-and I think I am borne out by what we know of the last eighteen months-and it would unquestionably raise the cost of many goods we have to import from the United States, because in effect we would be placing an additional ten per cent tariff across the board.
The second main criticism made of the government's program by hon. members both of the official opposition and of the C.C.F., and I think of the Social Credit group, was that we should have adopted the discriminatory principle, and that, in adopting the nondiscriminatory basis, we were jeopardizing the position of Great Britain with respect to sending us exports.
I, for one, attach great importance to the principle of non-discrimination. I believe it is a sound principle for any country to follow, and I think the government was right in adhering to that principle. I am sorry to say; no, I am not sorry to say, but in actual practice of course our policy is not nearly so non-discriminatory in fact as it is in form, because in selecting the articles to be prohibited, and the articles to be placed on quota, we have paid particular attention to those which come to us from sterling area countries.
May I say that explains why some articles, seemingly luxury articles, are included in the quota list, where in the majority of cases the source of supply is in non-dollar countries.
I asked for the figure this afternoon, and I am told that the prohibited list now covers only about two and a quarter million dollars

of United Kingdom imports. That is less than It per cent of the total imports from that country to Canada.

I make this assertion, and every hon. member will see in due course that it is borne out by the facts, that this program, instead of hindering imports from the United Kingdom, will stimulate them, because of the quota basis. Let us take textiles, as an outstanding example. Imports from the United States will be cut down to about one-third of last year's exports to Canada; whereas Great Britain can export 200 per cent of her last year's exports to this country. And that will apply, hon. members will find, in the case of a great many commodities.
The question was raised as to the protectionist feature of this legislation. Of course it is protectionist; it cannot be anything else. I have repeatedly said in my radio speeches, and I said it here, that is one of the things which the government regrets. But it is a necessity. I used the words, in speaking in Montreal, that these restrictions are an unmitigated evil, but a necessary evil.
There has been talk in this debate of economic domination by the United States. Let me say this, that a nation which loses its exchange reserves loses its independence. Let there be no mistake about that.
What we are considering in this bill is a method of preventing such an exchange reserve loss. My hon. friends opposite advocate a currency depreciation of ten per cent or more-"Take the exchange controls off, and let her rip". I do not subscribe to that at all. If we were to permit exchange depreciation to any substantial extent, the increase in the cost of living would be something that would make your hair curl. Anybody who says that in a country operating at full capacity, as we are today, even a ten per cent currency depreciation is not inflationary, is living in a world of fantasy.
I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the house. As I have said, I am not going to deal in detail with a number of the suggestions which have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite. For instance the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) suggested that we might start a Canadian stud book in Canada, and that this would bring in some United States dollars. I am not a racing man, but I shall look into the matter. However, I doubt very much if it would cure our exchange situation.
The attitude of the C.C.F. group I find a little harder to understand. The hon. member

Then, he referred to the adoption of the non-discriminatory principle. I have already dealt with that.
The third reason he gave for voting against the bill was that we do not propose to impose price ceilings on articles which are prohibited, or placed under quota. The fourth reason was the fear that the effect of these restrictive measures would create a highly protectionist position which it would be difficult to get out of. I can say this-

During the course of this debate there was some discussion as to what our exchange reserve position is today, that is to say, what are our official holdings of gold and United States dollars. I think it was the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins) who requested that I give up-to-date figures as to that matter. Let me say at once that, while I think it is only fair that v'hen this matter is before the house details of our position should be made clear to hon. members, for reasons which I have stated on previous occasions, I do not think as a general principle it is desirable to give too frequent statements of our exchange holdings. I believe the publication of these figures at too frequent intervals would serve only the selfish interests of speculators. It could not serve the public good. I propose now to give the details of our actual position and the trend in the last couple of months.
The house will recall that in my broadcast speech on November 17 last I pointed out that at the close of business on the previous Thursday, that is at November 13 or 14, our exchange holdings were down to slightly over $500 million. While we were imposing import
Foreign Exchange Conservation

restrictions of a reasonably extensive nature we realized that those' restrictions could not become effective overnight. We knew also, from the experience of other countries which had had to adopt similar measures, that because of the recognition of some existing orders and commitments the country's exchange reserves would probably fall for some time after the import restrictions were imposed. For those reasons we thought it was likely that our exchange reserves would fall to a figure approaching $400 million following the imposition of these import restrictions before they could become effective.
I am glad to say that actually the results have been a great deal better. At the end of November, as I think I have already reported to the house, our reserves had fallen to approximately $480 million, and the decline was then continuing. On December 17 the low point was reached of just under $461 million. However, we ended the year 1947 with total holdings of $502 million, and at the close of business yesterday, that is Thursday, January 29, our total holdings of gold and United States dollars were approximately $514 million, the exact figure being $513,884,563. As I have already said, I believe that that record is a very encouraging one.

There has been talk about the chaotic conditions which have resulted and so on. The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) referred to the fact that I had been over in England. If the people of this country who talk about hardship when they cannot get a head of lettuce or a dish of imported strawberries or some of these, other pleasant but somewhat unnecessary things would spend a week or two in enjoying the no doubt nutritious but singularly uninteresting diet they have in Great Britain or the still more uninteresting diet in many other places, I do not believe they would lay such strong emphasis on the hardships we are being asked to undergo in this country in order to live within our means or within our customer's means.
This measure is one to enable us to continue to play our part in assisting in the recovery of some of those countries to which I have referred. It is important that the people of this country should know the purposes of this measure and the reasons why it is being introduced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I move that the house do now adjourn. I am happy to say that I have now from all parties the names of the members of the select committee on the investigation of prices. The motion with respect to this committee will be the first order of business on Monday. Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 6.20 p.m.
